::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Task 1: Data Acquisition"}

## Task 1: Data Acquisition

```{r}
#| label: task1-data-acquisition
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Task 1 Code"
#| results: hide

# Load required packages
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)
library(readxl)
library(fs)
library(lubridate)
library(gt)

# Acquire Netflix What We Watched Reports
load_netflix_data <- function() {

  # Create the folder where Netflix data will be saved
  data_dir <- fs::path("data", "mp01")

  if (!fs::dir_exists(data_dir)) {
    fs::dir_create(
      data_dir,
      showWarnings = FALSE,
      recurse = TRUE
    )
  }

  # Netflix reporting webpages
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )

  # Specify the local Excel file paths
  local_paths <- fs::path(
    data_dir,
    paste0(names(NETFLIX_URLS), ".xlsx")
  )

  # Download only the files that are missing
  for (p in names(NETFLIX_URLS)) {

    local_file <- fs::path(
      data_dir,
      paste0(p, ".xlsx")
    )

    if (!fs::file_exists(local_file)) {

      webpage <- rvest::read_html(NETFLIX_URLS[[p]])

      excel_url <- webpage |>
        rvest::html_element(
          xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]"
        ) |>
        rvest::html_attr("href")

      if (length(excel_url) != 1 || is.na(excel_url)) {
        stop("Excel file not found for ", p)
      }

      excel_url <- xml2::url_absolute(
        excel_url,
        NETFLIX_URLS[[p]]
      )

      download.file(
        excel_url,
        local_file,
        quiet = TRUE,
        mode = "wb"
      )
    }
  }

  # Read and combine the seven reports
  tibble(
    period = names(NETFLIX_URLS),
    path = local_paths
  ) |>
    mutate(
      data = map(
        path,
        \(x) read_excel(
          x,
          skip = 3,
          na = "*"
        )
      ),
      data = map(
        data,
        \(x) x |>
          mutate(
            `Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)
          )
      )
    ) |>
    unnest(data) |>
    select(-path) |>

    # Create the reporting period dates
    mutate(
      year = str_sub(period, 1, 4),
      half = str_sub(period, start = 6),

      period_start = make_date(
        year,
        if_else(half == 1, 1, 7),
        1
      ),

      period_end = make_date(
        year,
        if_else(half == 1, 6, 12),
        if_else(half == 1, 30, 31)
      )
    ) |>

    # Exclude missing viewing hours
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |>

    # Convert runtime to minutes
    mutate(
      live_event = !is.na(Runtime) &
        str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"),

      clean_time = str_remove(
        Runtime,
        fixed("*")
      ),

      Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) +
        minute(hm(clean_time))
    ) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>

    # Clean runtime and title values
    mutate(
      Runtime = coalesce(
        Runtime,
        mean(Runtime, na.rm = TRUE)
      ),

      .by = Title,

      Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(
        Title,
        "Latin-ASCII"
      ),

      Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"),
      Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"),
      Title = str_trim(Title)
    ) |>
    filter(Title != "") |>

    # Keep the columns needed for the project
    select(
      year,
      period,
      period_start,
      period_end,
      Title,
      -half,
      Runtime,
      Views,
      `Hours Viewed`,
      `Release Date`,
      `Available Globally?`,
      live_event
    )
}

# Location of the saved cleaned dataset
cache_file <- fs::path(
  "data",
  "mp01",
  "netflix_clean.rds"
)

# Use the saved dataset if it exists
if (file.exists(cache_file)) {

  NETFLIX_DATA <- readRDS(cache_file)

} else {

  # Otherwise run the original data acquisition process
  NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()

}
```

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Task 2: Fix Column Titles"}


## Task 2: Fix Column Titles

```{r}
#| label: task2-fix-column-titles
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Task 2 Code"
#| results: hide

# Change column names to lowercase with underscores
# Skip renaming if the saved data already has clean names

if ("Title" %in% names(NETFLIX_DATA)) {

  NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
    rename(
      title = Title,
      runtime = Runtime,
      views = Views,
      hours_viewed = `Hours Viewed`,
      release_date = `Release Date`,
      available_globally = `Available Globally?`
    )

}
```

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Task 3: Fix Column Types"}

## Task 3: Fix Column Types

```{r}
#| label: task3-fix-column-types
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Task 3 Code"
#| results: hide

# Convert year to integer
NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(year)
  )

# Convert global availability to TRUE, FALSE, or NA
# Check whether the column is already logical
if (!is.logical(NETFLIX_DATA$available_globally)) {

  NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
    mutate(
      available_globally = case_when(
        available_globally == "Yes" ~ TRUE,
        available_globally == "No" ~ FALSE,
        TRUE ~ NA
      )
    )

}

# Save the cleaned data for future renders
saveRDS(
  NETFLIX_DATA,
  cache_file
)
```

### Random Sample of Netflix Titles

```{r}
#| label: task4-random-sample
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Random Sample Code"

# Select a random sample of ten observations
set.seed(9750)

netflix_sample <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  slice_sample(n = 10) |>
  select(
    period,
    title,
    runtime,
    views,
    hours_viewed,
    release_date,
    available_globally,
    live_event
  )

# Format the random sample into a table
netflix_sample |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Random Sample of Netflix Titles",
    subtitle = "Ten observations from the Netflix viewing dataset"
  ) |>
  gt::cols_label(
    period = "Reporting Period",
    title = "Netflix Title",
    runtime = "Runtime (Minutes)",
    views = "Views",
    hours_viewed = "Viewing Hours",
    release_date = "Release Date",
    available_globally = "Available Globally",
    live_event = "Live Event"
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = c(runtime, views, hours_viewed),
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_date(
    columns = release_date,
    date_style = "iso"
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_missing(
    columns = everything(),
    missing_text = "NA"
  ) |>
  gt::tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Source: Netflix What We Watched reports, 2023H1–2026H1."
  )
```


### 4. Missing Data Analysis

```{r}
#| label: task4-missing-data
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Missing Data Code"

# Calculate missing values for every column
missing_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(
    across(
      everything(),
      ~sum(is.na(.x))
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "missing_values"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    total_records = nrow(NETFLIX_DATA),
    missing_percentage = missing_values / total_records
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_values))

# Create a formatted missing-data table
missing_data |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Netflix Data Completeness",
    subtitle = "Missing observations by variable"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    variable = "Variable",
    missing_values = "Missing Values",
    total_records = "Total Records",
    missing_percentage = "Missing (%)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(missing_values, total_records),
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = missing_percentage,
    decimals = 1
  ) |>
  data_color(
    columns = missing_percentage,
    palette = c("#FFFFFF", "#F5B7B1", "#E50914")
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Source: Netflix What We Watched reports. Missing values are identified using is.na()."
  )
```
### Observations 

*Over half of the release dates are missing. This can affect comparisons between newer and older TV shows and movies. About one-third of the views are missing, which can affect comparisons across periods if the missing values are not evenly distributed. About one-fifth of runtime values are missing, which affects comparisons between TV shows and movies. Nearly all the other columns have complete data.*

### 5. Additional Data Quality Checks

```{r}
#| label: task4-quality-checks
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Quality Check Code"

# Check the dataset for potential data issues
quality_checks <- tibble(
  check = c(
    "Total Observations",
    "Unique Netflix Titles",
    "Reporting Periods",
    "Duplicate Title-Period Records",
    "Missing Titles",
    "Missing Viewing Hours",
    "Negative Viewing Hours",
    "Invalid Reported Runtimes"
  ),
  result = c(
    nrow(NETFLIX_DATA),
    n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$title),
    n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$period),
    nrow(NETFLIX_DATA) -
      nrow(distinct(NETFLIX_DATA, period, title)),
    sum(is.na(NETFLIX_DATA$title)),
    sum(is.na(NETFLIX_DATA$hours_viewed)),
    sum(NETFLIX_DATA$hours_viewed < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(
      NETFLIX_DATA$runtime <= 0,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )
)

quality_checks |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Netflix Data Quality Checks",
    subtitle = "Basic validation of the cleaned dataset"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    check = "Data Quality Check",
    result = "Result"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = result,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Source: Netflix What We Watched reports."
  )
```


### 6. Identify Duplicate Title Records

```{r}
#| label: task4-duplicate-records
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Duplicate Records Code"

# Identify titles appearing multiple times within a reporting period
duplicate_titles <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period, title) |>
  filter(n() > 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(period, title)

# Count the number of duplicate title-period combinations
duplicate_summary <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  count(period, title, name = "record_count") |>
  filter(record_count > 1) |>
  arrange(desc(record_count), period, title)

# Display the total number of duplicate combinations
nrow(duplicate_summary)

# Display examples of duplicate records
duplicate_titles |>
  select(
    period,
    title,
    runtime,
    views,
    hours_viewed,
    release_date,
    available_globally
  ) |>
  slice_head(n = 12) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Examples of Duplicate Netflix Title Records",
    subtitle = "Titles appearing more than once within the same reporting period"
  ) |>
  gt::cols_label(
    period = "Period",
    title = "Netflix Title",
    runtime = "Runtime (Minutes)",
    views = "Views",
    hours_viewed = "Viewing Hours",
    release_date = "Release Date",
    available_globally = "Available Globally"
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = c(runtime, views, hours_viewed),
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_date(
    columns = release_date,
    date_style = "iso"
  ) |>
  gt::tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Source: Netflix What We Watched reports, 2023H1–2026H1."
  )
```
### Observations 

*Some titles appear more than once, but not all of these records are exact duplicates. They may have different release dates or viewing hours. Different viewing hours are less concerning because the values can be added together. I am only removing rows that are exactly the same across every column.*

### Remove Exact Duplicate Records

```{r}
#| label: task4-remove-exact-duplicates
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Duplicate Removal Code"

# Count records before removing duplicates
rows_before <- nrow(NETFLIX_DATA)

# Count exact duplicate rows
exact_duplicates <- sum(duplicated(NETFLIX_DATA))

# Remove rows that are identical across every column
NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  distinct()

# Count records after removing duplicates
rows_after <- nrow(NETFLIX_DATA)

# Summarize the results
tibble(
  measure = c(
    "Records Before",
    "Exact Duplicates Removed",
    "Records After"
  ),
  count = c(
    rows_before,
    exact_duplicates,
    rows_after
  )
) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Netflix Data Deduplication",
    subtitle = "Exact duplicate rows removed across all columns"
  ) |>
  gt::cols_label(
    measure = "Measure",
    count = "Number of Records"
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = count,
    decimals = 0
  )
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Task 5: Exploratory Questions - Inline Values"}

```{r}
#| label: task5-inline-calculations
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Task 5 Code"
#| results: hide

# Load the package used to format the numbers
library(scales)


# Question 1: date range


# Find the first and last dates in the dataset
first_date <- min(NETFLIX_DATA$period_start, na.rm = TRUE)
last_date <- max(NETFLIX_DATA$period_end, na.rm = TRUE)



# Question 2: total unique titles


# Count each distinct title only once
total_titles <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(
    titles = n_distinct(title)
  ) |>
  pull(titles)



# Question 3: bridgerton universe


# Include titles containing Bridgerton
# This includes related titles mentioning Bridgerton
bridgerton_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(
    str_detect(
      title,
      regex("Bridgerton", ignore_case = TRUE)
    )
  ) |>
  summarise(
    total_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pull(total_hours)



# Question 4: stranger things seasons 1-5


# Identify the original series and numbered seasons
# Exclude spin-offs and companion productions
stranger_things_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(
    str_detect(
      title,
      regex("^Stranger Things", ignore_case = TRUE)
    )
  ) |>
  filter(
    str_detect(
      title,
      regex(
        "^Stranger Things(?:\\s*:\\s*Season\\s*[1-5]|\\s+Season\\s*[1-5]|\\s+[1-5])?$",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )
    )
  )

# Sum viewing hours for the original series
stranger_things_hours <- stranger_things_data |>
  summarise(
    total_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pull(total_hours)



# Question 5: top 10 titles in 2026H1


# Keep the 2026H1 reporting period
netflix_2026 <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(period == "2026H1")

# Calculate total viewing hours in 2026H1
total_hours_2026 <- netflix_2026 |>
  summarise(
    total_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pull(total_hours)

# Combine records belonging to the same title
title_hours_2026 <- netflix_2026 |>
  group_by(title) |>
  summarise(
    title_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(title_hours))

# Identify the ten most-watched titles
top10_titles_2026 <- title_hours_2026 |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

# Calculate top-ten share of total viewing hours
top10_share <- sum(top10_titles_2026$title_hours) /
  total_hours_2026


# Question 6: global availability


# Determine whether each unique title was ever
# available globally during the reporting periods
global_titles <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(title) |>
  summarise(
    known_availability = any(!is.na(available_globally)),
    globally_available = any(available_globally %in% TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(known_availability)

# Percentage of unique titles available globally
global_title_share <- global_titles |>
  summarise(
    share = mean(globally_available)
  ) |>
  pull(share)

# Exclude records where availability is unknown
global_hours_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(!is.na(available_globally))

# Percentage of viewing hours from globally available titles
global_hours_share <- global_hours_data |>
  summarise(
    share = sum(
      hours_viewed[available_globally],
      na.rm = TRUE
    ) / sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pull(share)

# Confirm calculations returned valid values
stopifnot(
  total_titles > 0,
  nrow(stranger_things_data) > 0,
  nrow(top10_titles_2026) == 10,
  is.finite(bridgerton_hours),
  is.finite(stranger_things_hours),
  is.finite(top10_share),
  is.finite(global_title_share),
  is.finite(global_hours_share)
)
```

### Question 1: What date range is covered by this data set?

The dataset covers the period from `r format(first_date, "%B %d, %Y")` through `r format(last_date, "%B %d, %Y")`.

### Question 2: How many different shows and movies are covered in this data set?

The dataset contains `r scales::comma(total_titles)` unique shows and movies across the seven reporting periods.

### Question 3: How many total hours have been spent watching shows from the Bridgerton universe?

The combined viewing hours for titles in the *Bridgerton* universe total `r scales::comma(bridgerton_hours)` hours, or approximately `r scales::number(bridgerton_hours / 1e9, accuracy = 0.01)` billion hours.

### Question 4: How many total hours have been spent watching the five seasons of Stranger Things? 

The five seasons of *Stranger Things* generated a combined `r scales::comma(stranger_things_hours)` viewing hours, excluding companion shows and spin-offs.

### Question 5: What percentage of total watch time was spent on the Top 10 titles of 2026H1?

The ten most-watched titles in 2026H1 accounted for `r scales::percent(top10_share, accuracy = 0.1)` of total viewing hours during that reporting period.

### Question 6: What fraction of Netflix’s catalog is globally available?

Across titles with known availability, `r scales::percent(global_title_share, accuracy = 0.1)` of unique titles were available globally during at least one reporting period.

When weighted by reported viewing hours, globally available content accounted for `r scales::percent(global_hours_share, accuracy = 0.1)` of viewing hours among records with known availability.

:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Task 6: Exploratory Questions - Table Answers"}


### Question 1: What Was the Top Title in Each Period?

```{r}
#| label: task6-top-titles
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Question 1 Code"

# Calculate viewing hours by title and period
title_viewership <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period, title) |>
  summarise(
    title_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Calculate total viewing hours for each period
period_totals <- title_viewership |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    period_hours = sum(title_hours),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Find the top title in each reporting period
top_titles <- title_viewership |>
  group_by(period) |>
  slice_max(
    title_hours,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(period_totals, by = "period") |>
  mutate(
    viewership_share = title_hours / period_hours
  ) |>
  arrange(period)

# Format the results
top_titles |>
  select(
    period,
    title,
    title_hours,
    viewership_share
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Netflix's Most-Watched Titles by Reporting Period",
    subtitle = "Viewing hours and share of total viewing time, 2023H1–2026H1"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Reporting Period",
    title = "Most-Watched Title",
    title_hours = "Viewing Hours",
    viewership_share = "Share of Total"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = title_hours,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = viewership_share,
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Source: Netflix What We Watched reports."
  )
```

#### Visualization: Top Title's Share of Viewing Hours

```{r}
#| label: task6-top-title-chart
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Question 1 Chart Code"
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(
  top_titles,
  aes(
    x = factor(
      period,
      levels = rev(sort(unique(period)))
    ),
    y = viewership_share
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    fill = "#E50914",
    width = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = stringr::str_trunc(title, width = 32)
    ),
    y = 0,
    hjust = -0.08,
    color = "white",
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 3.2
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = scales::percent(
        viewership_share,
        accuracy = 0.1
      )
    ),
    hjust = -0.15,
    color = "#333333",
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.20))
  ) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "Netflix's Biggest Hits by Reporting Period",
    subtitle = "Percentage of total viewing hours captured by the top title",
    x = "Reporting Period",
    y = "Share of Total Viewing Hours",
    caption = "Source: Netflix What We Watched reports"
  ) +

    ),

    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 1),
    plot.margin = margin(15, 25, 15, 15)
  )
```

### Question 2: How Has Netflix's Catalog Changed in Size Over Time?

```{r}
#| label: task6-catalog-size
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Question 2 Code"

# Keep one runtime per title in each period
# Use the largest available runtime for repeated listings
catalog_titles <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period, title) |>
  summarise(
    title_runtime = if (
      all(is.na(runtime))
    ) NA_real_ else max(runtime, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Calculate the number of titles and total runtime
catalog_size <- catalog_titles |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    number_of_titles = n(),
    total_runtime_hours = sum(
      title_runtime,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ) / 60,
    missing_runtime = sum(is.na(title_runtime)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(period)

# Format the results
catalog_size |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Netflix Catalog Size by Reporting Period",
    subtitle = "Number of reported titles and combined content runtime"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Reporting Period",
    number_of_titles = "Number of Titles",
    total_runtime_hours = "Total Runtime (Hours)",
    missing_runtime = "Titles Missing Runtime"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      number_of_titles,
      total_runtime_hours,
      missing_runtime
    ),
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Source: Netflix What We Watched reports. Each title is counted once per period; missing runtimes are excluded from runtime totals."
  )
```

### Question 3: Which Titles Have the Most Consistently High Viewership?

```{r}
#| label: task6-consistent-titles
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Question 3 Code"

# Calculate hours per title in each period
title_period_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(title, period) |>
  summarise(
    viewing_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Calculate viewing consistency statistics
title_consistency <- title_period_hours |>
  group_by(title) |>
  summarise(
    periods_present = n_distinct(period),
    average_hours = mean(viewing_hours),
    minimum_hours = min(viewing_hours),
    sd_hours = sd(viewing_hours),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    coefficient_variation = if_else(
      average_hours > 0,
      sd_hours / average_hours,
      NA_real_
    )
  )

# Require appearances in every reporting period
consistent_candidates <- title_consistency |>
  filter(periods_present == 7)

# Select titles with above-median average viewership
# Rank them by their lowest reporting-period viewership
consistent_titles <- consistent_candidates |>
  filter(
    average_hours >= median(
      consistent_candidates$average_hours
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(minimum_hours)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

# Format the table
consistent_titles |>
  select(
    title,
    average_hours,
    minimum_hours,
    sd_hours,
    coefficient_variation
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Netflix's Most Consistently Popular Titles",
    subtitle = "Titles appearing in all seven reporting periods"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    title = "Netflix Title",
    average_hours = "Average Viewing Hours",
    minimum_hours = "Minimum Viewing Hours",
    sd_hours = "Standard Deviation",
    coefficient_variation = "Variability (CV)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      average_hours,
      minimum_hours,
      sd_hours
    ),
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = coefficient_variation,
    decimals = 1
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Source: Netflix What We Watched reports. Titles are ranked by minimum viewing hours after requiring above-median average viewing hours and appearances in all seven periods."
  )
```

### Question 4: What Fraction of Viewing Time Was Spent on TV Shows vs. Movies?

```{r}
#| label: task6-tv-movies
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Question 4 Code"

# Exclude records with missing or invalid runtime
# Classify TV shows using runtime and title information
netflix_content <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(
    !is.na(runtime),
    is.finite(runtime),
    runtime > 0
  ) |>
  mutate(
    content_type = case_when(
      str_detect(
        title,
        regex("Season", ignore_case = TRUE)
      ) ~ "TV Show",
      runtime > 240 ~ "TV Show",
      TRUE ~ "Movie"
    )
  )

# Calculate viewing hours by content type
content_viewership <- netflix_content |>
  group_by(period, content_type) |>
  summarise(
    total_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(
    viewing_share = total_hours / sum(total_hours)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(period, content_type)

stopifnot(
  all(abs(
    content_viewership |>
      summarise(total_share = sum(viewing_share), .by = period) |>
      pull(total_share) - 1
  ) < 1e-10)
)

# Format the comparison
content_viewership |>
  select(
    period,
    content_type,
    total_hours,
    viewing_share
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Netflix Viewing Time: TV Shows vs. Movies",
    subtitle = "Share of viewing hours among titles with valid runtimes"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Reporting Period",
    content_type = "Content Type",
    total_hours = "Viewing Hours",
    viewing_share = "Share of Viewing"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = total_hours,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = viewing_share,
    decimals = 1
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Source: Netflix What We Watched reports. TV classification uses 'Season' in the title or runtime exceeding 240 minutes. Records with missing or invalid runtimes are excluded."
  )
```

### Question 5: How Does Live Content Compare to Pre-Recorded Content?

```{r}
#| label: task6-live-comparison
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Question 5 Code"

# Classify records using their live-event indicator
live_content <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(!is.na(live_event)) |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(
      live_event,
      "Live Event",
      "Pre-Recorded"
    )
  )

# Compare average, median, and top-tier viewing hours
live_comparison <- live_content |>
  group_by(content_type) |>
  summarise(
    number_of_records = n(),
    average_hours = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_hours = median(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    top_1_threshold = as.numeric(
      quantile(
        hours_viewed,
        0.99,
        na.rm = TRUE
      )
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    live_content |>
      group_by(content_type) |>
      summarise(
        top_1_average = mean(
          hours_viewed[
            hours_viewed >= quantile(
              hours_viewed,
              0.99,
              na.rm = TRUE
            )
          ],
          na.rm = TRUE
        ),
        .groups = "drop"
      ),
    by = "content_type"
  )

# Format the comparison table
live_comparison |>
  select(
    content_type,
    number_of_records,
    average_hours,
    median_hours,
    top_1_threshold,
    top_1_average
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Netflix Live vs. Pre-Recorded Content",
    subtitle = "Average and top-tier viewing performance, 2023H1–2026H1"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    content_type = "Content Type",
    number_of_records = "Number of Records",
    average_hours = "Average Viewing Hours",
    median_hours = "Median Viewing Hours",
    top_1_threshold = "99th Percentile",
    top_1_average = "Top 1% Average"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      number_of_records,
      average_hours,
      median_hours,
      top_1_threshold,
      top_1_average
    ),
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Source: Netflix What We Watched reports. The top 1% threshold is calculated separately within each category, using viewing hours per title-period record."
  )
```

## Task 7: Corporate Strategy Memo

```{r}
#| label: task7-supporting-calculations
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Corporate Strategy Memo Calculations"
#| results: hide

# Task 7: supporting calculations

# Use the NETFLIX_DATA dataset from Tasks 1-4
# Exact duplicate records have already been removed.


# 1. classify TV shows and movies

stopifnot(
  "content_type" %in% names(netflix_content),
  "viewing_share" %in% names(content_viewership)
)

# Minimum and maximum viewing shares
tv_share_range <- content_viewership |>
  filter(content_type == "TV Show") |>
  summarise(
    low = min(viewing_share),
    high = max(viewing_share)
  )

movie_share_range <- content_viewership |>
  filter(content_type == "Movie") |>
  summarise(
    low = min(viewing_share),
    high = max(viewing_share)
  )

# 2. top 10 titles in 2026H1

title_performance <- netflix_content |>
  group_by(period, content_type, title) |>
  summarise(
    title_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

top_titles_2026 <- title_performance |>
  filter(period == "2026H1") |>
  group_by(title) |>
  summarise(
    title_hours = sum(title_hours),
    content_type = first(content_type),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(title_hours)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)


# 3. TV vs. movie performance per title

average_content_performance <- title_performance |>
  group_by(period, content_type) |>
  summarise(
    number_of_titles = n(),
    average_hours_per_title = mean(title_hours),
    median_hours_per_title = median(title_hours),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

tv_movie_comparison <- average_content_performance |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(
      content_type == "TV Show",
      "TV_Show",
      "Movie"
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    period,
    content_type,
    average_hours_per_title,
    median_hours_per_title
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = content_type,
    values_from = c(
      average_hours_per_title,
      median_hours_per_title
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    average_tv_movie_ratio =
      average_hours_per_title_TV_Show /
      average_hours_per_title_Movie,

    median_tv_movie_ratio =
      median_hours_per_title_TV_Show /
      median_hours_per_title_Movie
  ) |>
  arrange(period)

tv_movie_ratio_2026 <- tv_movie_comparison |>
  filter(period == "2026H1") |>
  pull(average_tv_movie_ratio)


# 4. prepare franchise viewing data

make_season_data <- function(
    prefix,
    seasons,
    before,
    during
) {

  NETFLIX_DATA |>
    filter(
      period %in% c(before, during),

      str_detect(
        title,
        regex(
          paste0(
            "^",
            prefix,
            "(?:\\s*:?\\s*(?:Season\\s*)?[1-",
            seasons,
            "])?$"
          ),
          ignore_case = TRUE
        )
      )
    ) |>
    mutate(
      season_number = as.integer(
        str_extract(
          title,
          paste0("[1-", seasons, "]$")
        )
      ),

      season_number = coalesce(
        season_number,
        1L
      )
    ) |>
    group_by(season_number, period) |>
    summarise(
      viewing_hours = sum(
        hours_viewed,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      season_label = factor(
        paste0("Season ", season_number),
        levels = paste0(
          "Season ",
          seasons:1
        )
      ),

      reporting_window = factor(
        period,
        levels = c(before, during),
        labels = c(
          "Previous period",
          "New-season period"
        )
      ),

      viewing_millions = viewing_hours / 1000000
    )
}


# 5. stranger things

# Compare Seasons 1-4 in 2025H1 and 2025H2
st_data <- make_season_data(
  "Stranger Things",
  4,
  "2025H1",
  "2025H2"
)

st_period_totals <- st_data |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    total_hours = sum(
      viewing_hours,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

st_before <- st_period_totals |>
  filter(period == "2025H1") |>
  pull(total_hours)

st_after <- st_period_totals |>
  filter(period == "2025H2") |>
  pull(total_hours)

st_change <- st_after / st_before - 1


# 6. bridgerton

# Compare Seasons 1-3 in 2025H2 and 2026H1
bridgerton_data <- make_season_data(
  "Bridgerton",
  3,
  "2025H2",
  "2026H1"
)

bridgerton_period_totals <- bridgerton_data |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    total_hours = sum(
      viewing_hours,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

bridgerton_before <- bridgerton_period_totals |>
  filter(period == "2025H2") |>
  pull(total_hours)

bridgerton_after <- bridgerton_period_totals |>
  filter(period == "2026H1") |>
  pull(total_hours)

bridgerton_change <-
  bridgerton_after / bridgerton_before - 1


# 7. franchise chart function

plot_franchise <- function(
    data,
    new_season,
    franchise
) {

  ggplot(
    data,
    aes(
      x = viewing_millions,
      y = season_label,
      fill = reporting_window
    )
  ) +
    geom_col(
      position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
      width = 0.7
    ) +
    geom_text(
      aes(
        label = paste0(
          round(viewing_millions, 1),
          "M"
        )
      ),
      position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
      hjust = -0.12,
      fontface = "bold",
      size = 3.6
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = c(
        "Previous period" = "#444444",
        "New-season period" = "#E50914"
      )
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(
      labels = scales::label_comma(),
      expand = expansion(
        mult = c(0, 0.22)
      )
    ) +
    labs(
      title = paste0(
        franchise,
        ": Older Seasons and Season ",
        new_season
      ),
      subtitle = "Viewing hours across consecutive six-month periods",
      x = "Viewing Hours (Millions)",
      y = NULL,
      fill = NULL,
      caption = "Source: Netflix What We Watched reports; comparison does not establish causation"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 1)
    )
}


# 8. global vs. regional content

# Exclude records with missing availability
availability_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(!is.na(available_globally))

# Count each unique title only once across all periods
# If a title was ever marked globally available,
# classify it as globally available

unique_title_availability <- availability_data |>
  group_by(title) |>
  summarise(
    available_globally = any(available_globally),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    availability = if_else(
      available_globally,
      "Globally Available",
      "Regionally Available"
    )
  )

# Share of unique titles
title_share_data <- unique_title_availability |>
  count(
    availability,
    name = "number_of_titles"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    share = number_of_titles /
      sum(number_of_titles)
  )

# Share of viewing hours
hours_share_data <- availability_data |>
  mutate(
    availability = if_else(
      available_globally,
      "Globally Available",
      "Regionally Available"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(availability) |>
  summarise(
    total_hours = sum(
      hours_viewed,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    share = total_hours /
      sum(total_hours)
  )


# 9. global vs. regional inline values

regional_title_share <- title_share_data |>
  filter(availability == "Regionally Available") |>
  pull(share)

regional_hours_share <- hours_share_data |>
  filter(availability == "Regionally Available") |>
  pull(share)


# 10. verify calculations

stopifnot(
  nrow(st_data) == 8,
  nrow(bridgerton_data) == 6,
  length(st_change) == 1,
  length(bridgerton_change) == 1,
  is.finite(st_change),
  is.finite(bridgerton_change),
  st_before > 0,
  bridgerton_before > 0,
  length(global_title_share) == 1,
  length(regional_title_share) == 1,
  length(global_hours_share) == 1,
  length(regional_hours_share) == 1,
  abs(
    sum(title_share_data$share) - 1
  ) < 0.000001,
  abs(
    sum(hours_share_data$share) - 1
  ) < 0.000001,
  abs(global_title_share + regional_title_share - 1) < 0.000001,
  abs(global_hours_share + regional_hours_share - 1) < 0.000001
)
```

## Netflix Corporate Strategy Recommendation 

While Netflix offers a large collection of content, to maximize value to subscribers and minimize cost, they need to follow the Pareto Principle. Using their viewership history they should focus on the 20% of content that brings in 80% of viewership.  Netflix should prioritize creating original long-running franchises that keep viewers engaged over multiple years. People spend significantly more time watching TV shows than movies. Franchises keep viewers engaged for longer periods of time. Original content also keeps users connected to the platform and can be made available globally. Franchises also provide long-term value. When a new season is released, people often go back to watch earlier seasons of the franchise.

### Gini Coefficient Analysis

```{r}
#| label: task7-gini-calculations
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Gini Analysis Code"
#| results: hide

# 1. calculate the Gini coefficient


calculate_gini <- function(x) {

  x <- x[is.finite(x) & x >= 0]

  if (length(x) == 0 || sum(x) == 0) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }

  x <- sort(x)

  n <- length(x)

  (2 * sum(seq_along(x) * x) /
     (n * sum(x))) - (n + 1) / n
}

# Verify the professor's example
example_income <- c(20, 200, 0, 50, 40)

example_gini <- calculate_gini(example_income)

stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    example_gini,
    172 / 310,
    tolerance = 0.000001
  ))
)



# 2. raw viewing hours by title and period


# Combine viewing hours for titles that have
# multiple listings within a reporting period

gini_title_hours <- title_viewership |>
  rename(viewing_hours = title_hours)



# 3. Gini based on raw viewing hours


gini_raw <- gini_title_hours |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    number_of_titles = n(),
    total_hours = sum(viewing_hours),
    gini_raw = calculate_gini(viewing_hours),
    .groups = "drop"
  )



# 4. estimate runtime-adjusted views


# Exclude records with missing or invalid runtime
# Runtime is measured in minutes

gini_valid_runtime <- netflix_content |>
  filter(
    is.finite(hours_viewed),
    hours_viewed >= 0
  ) |>
  mutate(
    runtime_hours = runtime / 60,
    estimated_views = hours_viewed / runtime_hours
  )

# Combine repeated listings for each title-period
gini_normalized_titles <- gini_valid_runtime |>
  group_by(period, title) |>
  summarise(
    viewing_hours = sum(hours_viewed),
    estimated_views = sum(estimated_views),
    .groups = "drop"
  )



# 5. calculate runtime-adjusted Gini


# Calculate Gini using both viewing hours and
# estimated views on the same valid-runtime titles

gini_adjusted <- gini_normalized_titles |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    titles_with_runtime = n(),

    valid_runtime_hours = sum(viewing_hours),

    gini_hours_same_sample =
      calculate_gini(viewing_hours),

    gini_adjusted =
      calculate_gini(estimated_views),

    .groups = "drop"
  )



# 6. combine results


gini_results <- gini_raw |>
  left_join(
    gini_adjusted,
    by = "period"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    runtime_coverage =
      valid_runtime_hours / total_hours
  ) |>
  arrange(period)



raw_gini_2026 <- gini_results |>
  filter(period == "2026H1") |>
  pull(gini_raw)

# 8. top 10% of titles in 2026H1


gini_2026_titles <- gini_title_hours |>
  filter(period == "2026H1") |>
  arrange(desc(viewing_hours))

# Number of titles in the top decile
top_10_count <- ceiling(
  nrow(gini_2026_titles) * 0.10
)

# Total viewing hours for top 10%
top_10_hours <- gini_2026_titles |>
  slice_head(n = top_10_count) |>
  summarise(
    total = sum(viewing_hours)
  ) |>
  pull(total)

# Total viewing hours for all titles
all_2026_hours <- sum(
  gini_2026_titles$viewing_hours
)

top_10_hours_share <- top_10_hours / all_2026_hours



# 9. prepare the lorenz curve


# Sort 2026H1 titles from lowest to highest
# viewing hours

lorenz_2026 <- gini_2026_titles |>
  arrange(viewing_hours) |>
  mutate(
    cumulative_titles = row_number() / n(),

    cumulative_hours =
      cumsum(viewing_hours) / sum(viewing_hours)
  ) |>
  select(
    cumulative_titles,
    cumulative_hours
  )

# Add the origin using an explicit data frame
# No pipe placeholder is used

lorenz_origin <- tibble(
  cumulative_titles = 0,
  cumulative_hours = 0
)

lorenz_2026 <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  lorenz_origin,
  lorenz_2026
)

lorenz_2026 <- lorenz_2026 |>
  arrange(cumulative_titles)



# 10. prepare the Gini trend chart


gini_chart_data <- gini_results |>
  select(
    period,
    gini_raw,
    gini_hours_same_sample,
    gini_adjusted
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      gini_raw,
      gini_hours_same_sample,
      gini_adjusted
    ),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "gini"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    measure = case_when(
      measure == "gini_raw" ~
        "Viewing Hours (All Titles)",

      measure == "gini_hours_same_sample" ~
        "Viewing Hours (Valid Runtime)",

      measure == "gini_adjusted" ~
        "Runtime-Adjusted Views"
    ),

    period = factor(
      period,
      levels = sort(unique(gini_results$period))
    )
  )



# 11. verify the results


stopifnot(
  nrow(gini_results) == 7,

  nrow(gini_2026_titles) > 0,

  all(is.finite(gini_results$gini_raw)),

  all(is.finite(gini_results$gini_adjusted)),

  all(gini_results$gini_raw >= 0),

  all(gini_results$gini_raw <= 1),

  all(gini_results$gini_adjusted >= 0),

  all(gini_results$gini_adjusted <= 1),

  is.finite(top_10_hours_share),

  top_10_hours_share >= 0,

  top_10_hours_share <= 1,

  nrow(lorenz_2026) ==
    nrow(gini_2026_titles) + 1
)
```

```{r}
  )
```

The Gini coefficient shows how viewing hours are distributed across the unique titles on Netflix. If every title had the same number of viewing hours, the Gini coefficient would be 0. If all viewing hours went to just one TV show or movie, the coefficient would be 1. A number closer to 1 means that viewers spend most of their time watching a small number of titles, while a number closer to 0 means viewing hours are more evenly distributed.

Based on the data below, the viewing-hours Gini coefficient of `r round(raw_gini_2026, 3)` in 2026H1 indicates that a small number of titles account for a highly disproportionate amount of viewing hours.

#### Netflix Viewing Concentration by Title Percentile

```{r}
#| label: task7-viewing-concentration-table
#| echo: false


# Viewing concentration by title percentile


# Start with title-level viewing hours for 2026H1
# Sort from least watched to most watched
concentration_data <- gini_2026_titles |>
  arrange(viewing_hours) |>
  mutate(cumulative_hours = cumsum(viewing_hours))

# Count total titles and total viewing hours
total_concentration_titles <- nrow(concentration_data)

total_concentration_hours <- sum(
  concentration_data$viewing_hours,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

# Calculate shares for bottom 20% through 90%
concentration_table <- tibble(
  bottom_share = seq(0.20, 0.90, by = 0.10)
) |>
  mutate(
    top_share = 1 - bottom_share,

    # Number of titles included in the bottom group
    bottom_titles = floor(
      total_concentration_titles * bottom_share
    )
  )

# Calculate viewing hours for each bottom group
concentration_table <- concentration_table |>
  mutate(
    bottom_hours = concentration_data$cumulative_hours[bottom_titles],
    # Calculate bottom and top viewing shares
    bottom_hours_share =
      bottom_hours / total_concentration_hours,

    top_hours_share =
      1 - bottom_hours_share,

    # Create labels for both groups
    bottom_group = paste0(
      "Bottom ",
      scales::percent(bottom_share, accuracy = 1)
    ),

    top_group = paste0(
      "Top ",
      scales::percent(top_share, accuracy = 1)
    )
  )

stopifnot(
  all(abs(
    concentration_table$bottom_hours_share +
      concentration_table$top_hours_share - 1
  ) < 1e-10),
  abs(
    concentration_table$top_hours_share[
      concentration_table$top_group == "Top 10%"
    ] - top_10_hours_share
  ) < 1e-10
)

# Format the results


concentration_table |>
  select(
    bottom_group,
    bottom_hours_share,
    top_group,
    top_hours_share
  ) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Netflix Viewing Concentration",
    subtitle = "Share of total viewing hours by title percentile, 2026H1"
  ) |>
  gt::cols_label(
    bottom_group = "Least-Watched Titles",
    bottom_hours_share = "Share of Viewing Hours",
    top_group = "Most-Watched Titles",
    top_hours_share = "Share of Viewing Hours"
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_percent(
    columns = c(
      bottom_hours_share,
      top_hours_share
    ),
    decimals = 1
  ) |>
  gt::data_color(
    columns = top_hours_share,
    palette = c("#FFFFFF", "#F5B7B1", "#E50914")
  ) |>
  gt::tab_style(
    style = gt::cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = gt::cells_body(
      rows = top_group == "Top 10%"
    )
  ) |>
  gt::tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Source: Netflix What We Watched reports. Titles are ranked by viewing hours; top and bottom groups are complementary."
  )
```

The Pareto Principle states 80% of results come from 20% of the effort. Businesses perform better when they can concentrate on the areas they do well and spend less time and money on work that reaps fewer rewards. Netflix provides value to subscribers every hour they view content. Currently the top 20% of titles account for 79.3% of viewing hours. The Lorenz curve below highlights this unequal distribution of viewing hours.

#### Visualization 2: Lorenz Curve for 2026H1

```{r}
#| label: task7-lorenz-curve
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(
  lorenz_2026,
  aes(
    x = cumulative_titles,
    y = cumulative_hours
  )
) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#777777",
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_area(
    fill = "#E50914",
    alpha = 0.12
  ) +
  geom_line(
    color = "#E50914",
    linewidth = 1.4
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent(),
    limits = c(0, 1),
    breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent(),
    limits = c(0, 1),
    breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Netflix Viewing Hours: Lorenz Curve",
    subtitle = "Distribution of Viewing Hours Across Titles, 2026H1",
    x = "Cumulative Share of Titles (Least to Most Watched)",
    y = "Cumulative Share of Viewing Hours",
    caption = "Source: Netflix What We Watched reports. Dashed line represents perfect equality."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 15
    ),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 1)
  )
```

Overall, a small percentage of titles account for most viewing hours. Netlfix needs to continue focusing on producing popular original franchises that are globally available.
